---
title: "Bayesian linear regression"
execute:
  enabled: true

The Provo Gaussian linear model can be combined with a prior to produce a posterior distribution over regression lines. Recall from [posterior distributions](../statistical-inference/posterior-distributions.qmd) that updating multiplies a likelihood by a prior and then normalizes the product. The response model remains the Gaussian specification stated below.

The [Provo measurements](regression-models.qmd#provo-word-position-data) define each response as a word position mean of log first fixation durations among readers with a retained positive fixation. They define modeled cloze surprisal as the negative base 2 logarithm of a fitted cloze probability. Skipped reader by word trials do not enter that mean, and the available table retains passage grouping rather than reader identities.

Recall from [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) that the likelihood is the joint density of the fixed observed responses viewed as a function of unknown parameters. Its factorization uses [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd); its covariance matrix records [variances and covariances](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd). [Monte Carlo integration](../statistical-inference/monte-carlo-integration.qmd) approximates posterior integrals by averaging over draws. A [residual](residuals.qmd) remains observed minus fitted response, now evaluated across posterior draws when uncertainty is propagated.

We will proceed in three steps. First, we choose a prior that permits a **closed
form update**, meaning that a finite sequence of algebraic operations gives the
posterior parameters. Second, we derive those updated parameters. Finally, we
use them to compute posterior summaries and fitted means.

The basic idea is the same as in the earlier [Beta--Binomial update](../statistical-inference/conjugate-priors.qmd): we begin with a probability distribution over possible parameter values, use the observed responses to reweight those values, and normalize. Regression adds several coefficients and an unknown residual variance, so the bookkeeping uses vectors and matrices. We will begin with a one-coefficient calculation each time the matrix notation would otherwise hide the operation.

$$
\mathbf Y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I).
$$

What changes is that uncertainty about $\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\sigma^2$ is represented before and after observing the responses.

## Choosing a prior family

A prior family is **conjugate** when multiplying its density by the likelihood produces a posterior in the same family. Conjugacy does not remove the need to justify a prior. It makes the update algebra visible because the posterior can be described by a new set of parameters rather than by a new functional form.

Why condition the coefficient prior on $\sigma^2$? Imagine two otherwise identical regression problems. In one, responses cluster tightly around their lines; in the other, they vary widely. Scaling the prior coefficient covariance by $\sigma^2$ lets the same dimensionless prior specification expand or contract with the residual scale. This coupling is what yields the closed-form update below.

The **inverse gamma distribution** is supported on positive values, which makes
it available as a distribution for the variance $\sigma^2$. We use a
normal--inverse-gamma specification: conditionally on $\sigma^2$, the
coefficient vector is multivariate normal, while $\sigma^2$ has an inverse gamma
distribution.

$$
\boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma^2
\sim
\mathcal N(\mathbf b_0,\sigma^2\mathbf V_0)
$$

and

$$
\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{InverseGamma}(a_0,d_0).
$$

We use the **shape--scale parameterization**. Here $a_0$ is the shape parameter
that controls the power on $\sigma^2$, and $d_0$ is the scale parameter that
controls exponential decay through $d_0/\sigma^2$. Its density kernel is

$$
p(\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)}
\exp\left(-\frac{d_0}{\sigma^2}\right),
$$

Its mean is $d_0/(a_0-1)$ when $a_0>1$. Conditional conjugacy is useful here because it makes every updating step visible. Other prior families remain available and will generally require a different computational strategy. When we later discuss [coefficient shrinkage](ridge-regression.qmd#penalties-and-priors), we will derive why a zero centered normal prior gives the ridge estimate as its posterior mode and why a zero centered Laplace prior gives the lasso estimate. Thus alternative coefficient priors change both posterior uncertainty and the form of regularization represented by the posterior mode. Software packages use different inverse gamma parameterizations, so we display the kernel to make our convention explicit.

## From likelihood and prior to posterior

The basic algebra is **completing the square**: rewriting a quadratic so that
its center is visible. Begin with one coefficient and suppress the common scale
factor. Combining one squared data discrepancy with a normal prior discrepancy
gives

$$
(y-\beta)^2+\frac{(\beta-b_0)^2}{v_0}
=
\left(1+\frac{1}{v_0}\right)\beta^2
-2\left(y+\frac{b_0}{v_0}\right)\beta
+\text{terms without }\beta.
$$

Write \(A=1+1/v_0\) and \(h=y+b_0/v_0\). Then

$$
A\beta^2-2h\beta
=
A\left(\beta-\frac{h}{A}\right)^2
-\frac{h^2}{A}.
$$

The coefficient \(A\) is the **precision**, the inverse of the variance, and
\(h\) is the precision-weighted total that combines the prior center with the
data. Their ratio \(h/A\) is the updated center. For several coefficients, the
same operation replaces the scalar precision $A$ with a matrix and the
precision-weighted total $h$ with a vector.

The likelihood kernel is

$$
p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma^2)
\propto
(\sigma^2)^{-n/2}
\exp\left[
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^\top
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)
\right].
$$

Multiplying by the conditional normal prior adds the quadratic

$$
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_0)^\top
\mathbf V_0^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_0).
$$

Collect the terms involving $\boldsymbol\beta$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\boldsymbol\beta^\top
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X+\mathbf V_0^{-1})
\boldsymbol\beta\\
&\quad-2\boldsymbol\beta^\top
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y+\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0)
+\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Define

$$
\mathbf V_n^{-1}=\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X,
\qquad
\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
=\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y.
$$

Thus \(\mathbf V_n^{-1}\) is the posterior **precision matrix**, and
\(\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y\) is the
corresponding precision-weighted total. Multiplying that vector by the
covariance \(\mathbf V_n\) recovers the posterior center \(\mathbf b_n\), just
as \(h/A\) did in the scalar calculation.

Completing the square yields

$$
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_n)^\top
\mathbf V_n^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf b_n)
+
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n.
$$

The first term is the kernel of the updated conditional normal distribution.
The second term contains no $\boldsymbol\beta$, so it becomes part of the updated
inverse gamma scale $d_n$. Thus the posterior parameters are the quantities left
by completing the square.

The posterior is again normal--inverse-gamma, with

$$
\mathbf V_n
=
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1},
$$

$$
\mathbf b_n
=
\mathbf V_n
(\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0+\mathbf X^\top\mathbf y),
$$

$$
a_n=a_0+\frac n2,
$$

and

$$
d_n
=
d_0+\frac12
\left(
\mathbf y^\top\mathbf y
+\mathbf b_0^\top\mathbf V_0^{-1}\mathbf b_0
-\mathbf b_n^\top\mathbf V_n^{-1}\mathbf b_n
\right).
$$

## Computing the posterior

Before drawing all coefficients, begin with a vector \(\mathbf z\) whose
coordinates are independent standard normal random variables. A matrix
\(\mathbf L\) can mix those coordinates into a new deviation vector
\(\boldsymbol\delta=\mathbf L\mathbf z\). The covariance of the result is

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\boldsymbol\delta]
=
\mathbf L\operatorname{Var}[\mathbf z]\mathbf L^{\mathsf T}
=
\mathbf L\mathbf L^{\mathsf T}.
$$

As in [matrix multiplication](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd#vectors-matrices-and-covariance),
each coordinate of the result is a sum of scalar products. We will use the
covariance estimated from the observed Provo responses and plot the resulting
posterior coefficient draws below.

We call a lower-triangular mixing matrix with this property a **Cholesky
factor**. In general, \(\mathbf L\) satisfies
\(\mathbf V_n=\mathbf L\mathbf L^{\mathsf T}\). R's `chol(Vn)` returns the
upper-triangular transpose \(\mathbf R=\mathbf L^{\mathsf T}\). Because the code
stores independent draws as rows, multiplying them on the right by
\(\mathbf R\) gives covariance
\(\mathbf R^{\mathsf T}\mathbf R=\mathbf V_n\).

```{r}
#| label: fit-provo-bayesian-regression
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)
provo$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  provo$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)

ols_fit <- lm(mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_c, data = provo)
X <- model.matrix(ols_fit)
y <- provo$mean_log_ffd
residual_scale <- summary(ols_fit)$sigma

b0 <- c(mean(y), 0)
V0 <- diag(c(
  (2 * sd(y) / residual_scale)^2,
  (2 * sd(y) / (sd(provo$cloze_surprisal_c) * residual_scale))^2
))
a0 <- ncol(X) + 1
d0 <- (a0 - 1) * residual_scale^2

Vn <- solve(solve(V0) + crossprod(X))
bn <- drop(Vn %*% (solve(V0) %*% b0 + crossprod(X, y)))
an <- a0 + nrow(provo) / 2
dn <- as.numeric(
  d0 + .5 * (
    crossprod(y) +
      t(b0) %*% solve(V0) %*% b0 -
      t(bn) %*% solve(Vn) %*% bn
  )
)

set.seed(20261019)
n_draws <- 4000L
sigma2_draws <- 1 / rgamma(n_draws, shape = an, rate = dn)
beta_noise <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_draws * ncol(X)),
  nrow = n_draws
) %*% chol(Vn)
beta_draws <- matrix(
  bn,
  nrow = n_draws,
  ncol = ncol(X),
  byrow = TRUE
) + sweep(beta_noise, 1, sqrt(sigma2_draws), `*`)
colnames(beta_draws) <- colnames(X)

slope_interval <- quantile(
  beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"],
  c(.025, .975)
)

stopifnot(
  all(is.finite(beta_draws)),
  all(is.finite(sigma2_draws)),
  slope_interval[[1]] < slope_interval[[2]]
)

data.frame(
  posterior_mean_slope = mean(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]),
  posterior_sd_slope = sd(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]),
  lower = slope_interval[[1]],
  upper = slope_interval[[2]]
)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-posterior-coefficient-covariance
#| fig-cap: "Joint posterior draws for the Provo intercept and surprisal slope. The shape comes from the covariance updated with the observed Provo responses."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of posterior intercept and slope draws forming a narrow tilted cloud."

posterior_coefficients <- data.frame(
  intercept = beta_draws[, "(Intercept)"],
  surprisal_slope = beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]
)

ggplot(posterior_coefficients, aes(intercept, surprisal_slope)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2C6E9B", alpha = 0.08, size = 0.6) + # dqr-allow: plot-aesthetic
  labs(
    x = "Posterior intercept draw",
    y = "Posterior surprisal-slope draw"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The tilted cloud shows how uncertainty in the two coefficients varies together after updating with the Provo responses. The Cholesky factor in the code creates exactly this covariance when it transforms independent standard normal draws.

The code mirrors the algebra: `Vn` inverts prior precision plus data precision;
`bn` multiplies that covariance by the precision weighted total from the prior and data; `an`
adds $n/2$; and `dn` is the constant left after completing the square. Because
$1/\sigma^2\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(a_n,d_n)$ under this parameterization,
`1 / rgamma(..., rate = dn)` generates inverse-gamma draws.

Scaling the transformed standard-normal vector by the sampled \(\sigma\) and
adding \(\mathbf b_n\) produces one draw from the conditional multivariate
normal posterior.

The 4,000 draws determine the Monte Carlo precision of our summaries. They do
not enter the inferential assumptions. For a posterior mean, simulation error is
approximately the posterior draw SD divided by $\sqrt{4000}$ because these
conjugate draws are independent. More draws reduce numerical error but do not
change the posterior distribution.

The posterior mean slope is `r sprintf("%.6f", mean(beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"]))`, with a central interval from `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_interval[[1]])` to `r sprintf("%.6f", slope_interval[[2]])`.

The coefficient prior location and scale use the observed Provo response and predictor scales. The inverse gamma shape is one plus the observed design dimension, and its scale sets the prior mean of $\sigma^2$ to the OLS residual variance. These priors depend on the data and are useful for connecting conjugate algebra to regression, but they were not specified independently for a confirmatory analysis.

The following prior predictive calculation makes that limitation visible. It draws parameters from a prior calibrated to these data and a response at centered surprisal before conditioning on the likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: check-provo-prior-predictive
set.seed(20261018)
n_prior_draws <- 1000L
prior_sigma2 <- 1 / rgamma(n_prior_draws, shape = a0, rate = d0) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
prior_beta_noise <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_prior_draws * ncol(X)),
  nrow = n_prior_draws
) %*% chol(V0)
prior_beta <- matrix(
  b0,
  nrow = n_prior_draws,
  ncol = ncol(X),
  byrow = TRUE
) + sweep(prior_beta_noise, 1L, sqrt(prior_sigma2), `*`)
colnames(prior_beta) <- colnames(X)
prior_mean_at_center <- prior_beta[, "(Intercept)"]
prior_response_at_center <- prior_mean_at_center +
  rnorm(n_prior_draws, sd = sqrt(prior_sigma2))

data.frame(
  quantity = c("mean at centered surprisal", "new response at centered surprisal"),
  lower = c(
    quantile(prior_mean_at_center, .025),
    quantile(prior_response_at_center, .025)
  ),
  median = c(
    median(prior_mean_at_center),
    median(prior_response_at_center)
  ),
  upper = c(
    quantile(prior_mean_at_center, .975),
    quantile(prior_response_at_center, .975)
  )
)
```

A [prior predictive check](../statistical-inference/prior-predictive-distributions.qmd) ordinarily precedes looking at the responses. Here it documents the implications of a prior already calibrated to those responses; it cannot retroactively make the prior independent of the sample.

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-bayesian-regression
#| fig-cap: "Provo positions with the posterior mean line and a central posterior interval for the conditional mean."
grid <- data.frame(
  cloze_surprisal_bits = seq(
    min(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    max(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits),
    length.out = 160L
  )
)
grid$cloze_surprisal_c <-
  grid$cloze_surprisal_bits - mean(provo$cloze_surprisal_bits)
mu_draws <- outer(
  beta_draws[, "cloze_surprisal_c"],
  grid$cloze_surprisal_c,
  `*`
)
mu_draws <- sweep(mu_draws, 1, beta_draws[, "(Intercept)"], `+`)
grid$posterior_mean <- colMeans(mu_draws)
grid$lower <- apply(mu_draws, 2, quantile, probs = .025)
grid$upper <- apply(mu_draws, 2, quantile, probs = .975)

point_opacity <- 0.2
interval_opacity <- 0.2
ggplot(provo, aes(cloze_surprisal_bits, mean_log_ffd)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = grid,
    aes(x = cloze_surprisal_bits, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#2C6E9B",
    alpha = interval_opacity
  ) +
  geom_point(color = "grey65", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid,
    aes(y = posterior_mean),
    color = "#2C6E9B",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Modeled cloze surprisal (bits)",
    y = "Mean log first fixation duration"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The posterior therefore represents uncertainty for the aggregated position likelihood. Participant responses remain unavailable, and a causal interpretation would require a research design that supports it.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which part of the model is shared with OLS?
2. Why do these priors fail to support a confirmatory analysis?
3. Why are predictions computed for every posterior draw?
4. Which data limitation survives the Bayesian formulation?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The Gaussian linear response model, including the straight conditional mean and common independent residual variance, is shared with OLS. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The coefficient and variance priors are calibrated from the observed predictor, response, and OLS residual scales rather than specified independently before seeing the data. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Evaluating the fitted mean within every joint draw propagates posterior covariance among coefficients into uncertainty about the prediction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The data still contain position summaries aggregated across readers, so individual responses and dependence among participants remain unavailable. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
